CurrentLocation: In situ, Tel Hazor National Park, Israel; Israel Museum, Jerusalem
Description: The largest biblical-period mound in Israel, excavated by Yigael Yadin in 1955-58, revealing a great Late Bronze Age city with temples and royal buildings, a destruction layer by fire, and a six-chambered gate like Megiddo's. Hazor was 'head of all those kingdoms' in Joshua's day and was fortified again in the monarchy period.
BiblicalSignificance: Hazor's burned Bronze Age layer fits its biblical description as the one northern city Joshua burned, though the exact dating and identity of its destroyers are debated. Together with its Solomonic-era gate, Hazor spans the story from conquest to kingdom, showing God's people planted in a land of real cities and real kings.
Interpretations: Scholars debate Hazor’s Solomonic gate and the extent of its tenth-century fortifications, as with Megiddo; the city’s importance in Joshua and Judges is not in doubt, but which stones are Solomon’s is.
